title: 🙅‍♂️ Refusin’ Texas
body_text: After launching its $499 AI-powered CameraJet toothbrush earlier this month, things haven’t been running smoothly for Dyson: the company was forced to withdraw the impressive (and impressively expensive) model from certain markets , as customers across the world took to social media to complain about various faults. Execs were initially tight-lipped about what exactly was going wrong with the CameraJet — which was trained on 470,000 dental images, has a 100,000-pixel macro lens, and jets short bursts of water into affected areas of the mouth like a water flosser — but have now told Bloomberg , presumably through gritted teeth, that “water seepage” was behind the malfunctioning early batch of brushes. There are songs that become so ubiquitous in modern life that they pass unchallenged into the modern music canon and wider public consciousness; trotted out for mass singalongs when the occasion demands: “All I Want for Christmas Is You,” before we’ve even taken Halloween decorations down; “Seven Nation Army,” at literally any sporting event anywhere in the world; “Wonderwall,” when the party has taken one too many wrong turns and the inevitable guitar is wielded. Although it’s now 24 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100, Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas,” most people agree, is not one of those songs. The song’s undeniable hook and the country-pop songstress’s sultry vocals aside, vast swaths of the music-listening public are queuing up to announce, sometimes proudly , that they’ve never heard the longest-reigning number one of all time. That might have something to do with how a lot of us have started finding new music. Billboard staff writer Kyle Denis says he isn’t surprised by the idea that there’s a song at the top of the charts for six months that a lot of people have never knowingly heard, as mainstream culture splinters into “incredibly optimized and hyper-individualized algorithmic silos and digital echo chambers.” That theory bears out in the responses to a YouGov survey conducted and published earlier this month. According to the poll, 59% of US adults who listen to music more than they did last year discover new music through streaming service recommendations, while 52% are finding songs via social media and music blogs. That marks a clear shift toward personal methods of picking up new music of late, as more traditional methods of song discovery like listening to the radio, music TV channels, and recommendations from family and friends slip down the list. As the monoculture recedes further into the rearview mirror with algorithms and for-you pages corroding the shared cultural experience that radio stations and mainstream television once helped to cultivate, it’s little wonder that we live in a world where a lot of Americans couldn’t begin to hum the melody of (on paper) one of the biggest songs in modern music. Whether or not you had an active choice in “Choosin’ Texas” becoming the song of 2026, you should probably get comfortable with the idea of megahits you’ve never heard before. Expectations are high as Micron Technology , the American chipmaker that’s become central to the artificial intelligence memory boom, prepares to report Q4 earnings results on today after the bell. Micron and its semiconductor peers have benefited from surging demand from AI hyperscalers such as Microsoft , Amazon , and Meta combined with industry-wide supply shortages. This tight market environment has given chipmakers strong pricing power, driving sharp sequential price increases. “We see the setup as constructive with multiple beat-and-raise levers still in play against a memory backdrop that remains structurally tight across both DRAM and NAND,” JP Morgan analysts wrote in a Monday note. Per analysts polled by FactSet, Micron is expected to report: $51.3 billion in revenue, including $39.8 billion from DRAM and $12.2 billion from NAND, the two kinds of memory chips Micron sells. That’s above the company’s guidance for revenue, which is between $49 billion to $51 billion. Adjusted earnings per share of $31.72. The company’s guidance for that metric as of its last report is between $30 and $32. To put the AI memory boom into perspective: Micron reported $11.3 billion in revenue and $3.03 in adjusted earnings per share in the same quarter last year. Beyond the quarterly numbers, JPMorgan noted, investors will also be looking for updates on Micron’s push to lock more customers into longer-term supply deals, as well as whether the company could soon put more cash toward buying back its own stock. With 95% of analysts having a “buy” rating on the stock, it's not exactly a hot take to predict that the earnings results will be bullish for the stock. title: 🩸 Red dye might not be enough
body_text: Being in the hospital is stressful enough, whether you’re a patient, loved one of a patient, or a staff member. And there’s one thing that sets everyone in a hospital even more on edge: the relentless, never-ending, cacophony of beeps. Most of the beeping beeps and ringing alarms don’t actually mean anyone needs to do anything – cue Homer Simpson’s sonically abusive invention, the deafening " Everything is OK alarm ” – which means doctors and nurses tend to tune them out. In most cases, that’s not a problem, but when it is a problem, it’s a problem . So, The Wall Street Journal reports , a Stanford University hospital sorted through the whole gamut of audible alerts in the monitoring equipment it uses and worked to cut out those that were unactionable or likely to quickly and harmless self-correct. The result? As much as a whooping 82% reduction in beeps. Even better, nurses said that they were better at actually responding to patient needs. Stocks dropped on Monday as Treasury yields rose. If you’ve driven a Ford – or any other type of internal combustion vehicle – lately , you’ve probably noticed that gas is expensive. Really expensive. Prices at the pump are up almost $1.50 per gallon since the US attacked Iran in late February. Things look even worse if you drive a truck, tractor or anything that runs on diesel, with the national average price per gallon sitting at $6.45, per AAA . Before the war, a gallon of diesel was just $3.75 . Diesel’s surge is pushing transportation and farming costs higher, contributing to the persistently high inflation that is the bane of politicians, consumers, and central bankers alike. To bring diesel prices down, the White House tried seeking voluntary diesel export limits from refiners last week, Reuters reported . Beyond asking nicely, a full export ban has also been mulled, not least by President Donald Trump, who took his own administration somewhat by surprise by publicly saying he supported the idea . Also gaining traction in the White House: slashing taxes on so-called red dyed diesel. Federal taxes for regular, un-dyed diesel sit at just under a quarter a gallon. Red-dyed diesel, which is distinguished by the addition of – you guessed it – red dye, can only be used in off-road activities like farming and power generation, is subject to a mere penny a gallon federal tax. The idea under consideration is to allow red dyed diesel to be used for on-road vehicles. A full-scale ban on diesel exports would likely lead rather quickly to domestic oversupply, which would cause refiners to cut production, leading rather quickly to scarcity domestically while drastically reducing supplies in Europe, industry officials have argued. Allowing wider use of red-dyed diesel might not have much of an effect on prices. "I can't ⁠think that this would have any impact at all," Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, told Reuters . "It's simply diesel with red dye added that's not taxed.
